Rambold ${ }^{9}$, Joerg M. Buescher ${ }^{10}$, Bernd Kammerer ${ }^{4,6,8}$, Nico Lachmann ${ }^{11}$, Marco Prinz ${ }^{7,8,12,13}$, Olaf Groß ${ }^{7,8,12,13}$, Edward J. Pearce ${ }^{10}$, Burkhard Becher ${ }^{3 \dagger}$, Philipp Henneke ${ }^{1,5,13 *}$ (D)
The skin needs to balance tolerance of colonizing microflora with rapid detection of potential pathogens. Flexible response mechanisms would seem most suitable to accommodate the dynamic challenges of effective antimicrobial defense and restoration of tissue homeostasis. Here, we dissected macrophage-intrinsic mechanisms and microenvironmental cues that tune macrophage signaling in localized skin infection with the colonizing and opportunistic pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. Early in skin infection, the cytokine granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) produced by $\gamma \delta$ T cells and hypoxic conditions within the dermal microenvironment diverted macrophages away from a homeostatic M-CSF- and hypoxia-inducible factor 1a (HIF-1a)-dependent program. This allowed macrophages to be metabolically rewired for maximal inflammatory activity, which requires expression of Irg1 and generation of itaconate, but not HIF-1a. This multifactorial macrophage rewiring program was required for both the timely clearance of bacteria and for the provision of local immune memory. These findings indicate that immunometabolic conditioning allows dermal macrophages to cycle between antimicrobial activity and protection against secondary infections. ## INTRODUCTION The skin hosts a dynamic microflora composed of fungi and bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus, which colonizes mucocutaneous surfaces of the anterior nares and moist skin in up to $30 \%$ of humans, who are mostly asymptomatic (1). Colonization frequencies are particularly high at the beginning of life, when the individual microflora is established (2). Staphylococcal strains are usually largely unchanged in a host over long periods. Yet S. aureus has high pathogenic potential and as such is a leading cause of acute bacterial skin infections (3). Thus, a carefully balanced and highly flexible host-microbe interface is essential for coexistence. Children with cellular innate immunodeficiency, such as genetic aberration in Toll-like (TLR) and interleukin-1 (IL-1) receptor signaling (IRAK4/MyD88 deficiency), are exceedingly susceptible to $S$. aureus infections, underlining the importance of innate immunity [^0]for infection control $(4,5)$. In line with this, tissue-resident macrophages (Macs), the most abundant immune cell type in the resting dermis, are key for controlling S. aureus skin infection (3, 6). Deficiencies in dermal Macs or MyD88 are similar with respect to impaired bacterial clearance and dysregulated neutrophil recruitment (7), and dermal Macs mediate transient innate immune memory with enhanced response to secondary S. aureus infection (8). Whereas a central role for dermal Macs in S. aureus defense has been established, the molecular and cellular dynamics, and functional hierarchies of heterocellular networks around Macs in skin infection, have not been resolved. In resting skin, dermal Macs consist of at least three definable subsets with discrete renewal patterns involving cells from primitive and definitive hematopoiesis (9-13). Macs continually survey and interact with the microenvironment and can undergo drastic changes during skin infection via coactivation and recruitment of circulating immune cells. Furthermore, the bacterial infection has high metabolic costs with altered energy and nutrient availability due to localized hypoxia, malperfusion (14), and nutrient competition between immune cells and invading pathogens $(15,16)$. Consequently, dermal Macs maintain high plasticity to respond to the variable microenvironment. The majority of tissue-resident Macs, including dermal Macs $(9,17)$, rely on macrophage colony-stimulating factor (MCSF) receptor signaling for their maintenance during homeostasis. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), on the other hand, is largely dispensable in steady state for most tissue Macs, with the notable exception of alveolar Macs $(18,19)$, but is relevant at sites of tissue inflammation (20) or bacterial infections (21-24). GM-CSF exerts immunomodulatory effects by boosting glycolysis in monocytes to drive cytokine production $(23,25)$, highlighting a link between GM-CSF in the microenvironment and alterations in carbohydrate metabolism. Macs generated in vitro will, upon microbial activation, increase the expression of the [^0]: ${ }^{\dagger}$ Institute for Immunodeficiency, Center for Chronic Immunodeficiency, Medical Center and Faculty of Medicine, University of Freiburg, 79106 Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{2}$ Faculty of Biology, University of Freiburg, 79104 Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{3}$ Institute of Experimental Immunology, University of Zurich, CH-8057 Zurich, Switzerland. ${ }^{4}$ Spemann Graduate School of Biology and Medicine, University of Freiburg, 79104 Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{5}$ Center for Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, University Medical Center, 79106 Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{6} 1$ Core Competence Metabolomics, Institute of Organic Chemistry, University of Freiburg, 79104 Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{7}$ Institute of Neuropathology, Medical Center and Faculty of Medicine, University of Freiburg, Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{8}$ Signalling Research Centre's BIOSS and CIBSS, University of Freiburg, 79104 Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{9}$ Department of Developmental Immunology, Max-Planck-Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics, Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{10}$ Department of Immunometabolism, Max-Planck-Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics, Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{11}$ Department of Pediatric Pneumology, Allergology and Neonatology and Cluster of Excellence RESIST (EXC 2155), Hannover Medical School, 30625 Hannover, Germany. ${ }^{12}$ Center for Basics in NeuroModulation (NeuroModulBasics), Faculty of Medicine, University of Freiburg, 79106 Freiburg, Germany. ${ }^{13}$ CIBSS-Center for Integrative Biological Signaling Studies, University of Freiburg, 79104 Freiburg, Germany. *Corresponding author. Email: philipp.henneke@uniklinik-freiburg.de $\dagger$ These authors contributed equally to this work. $\ddagger$ These authors contributed equally to this work.transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor $1 \alpha$ (HIF-1 $\alpha$ ) to drive aerobic glycolysis and down-regulate oxidative phosphorylation in favor of reactive oxygen species generation $(26,27)$. In contrast to thorough in vitro studies on Mac metabolism affecting immune functions, the link between dynamic cellular alterations during clearance of infection and reestablishment of tissue homeostasis remains largely elusive. Here, we show that dermal Macs engage a dynamic and multifaceted metabolic program during skin infection. In response to S. aureus and local hypoxia, homeostatic M-CSF-conditioned dermal Macs initially required HIF-1 $\alpha$ and generated energy through glycolysis. The switch to sustained glycolysis was driven by T cell-derived GM-CSF, which unleashed an alternative hypoxia Mac program that was HIF-1 $\alpha$ independent and contributed to immune memory acquisition. This program further involved the up-regulation of $\operatorname{Irg1}$ (immune responsive gene 1) and itaconate production, which were linked to the resolution of inflammation. Interference with any aspect of this stepwise cellular tuning delayed bacterial clearance and boosted tissue inflammation. ## RESULTS ## Dermal Macs undergo cellular reprogramming during $S$. aureus infection In staphylococcal skin infection, the complex kinetic changes in Mac and granulocyte composition cannot be sufficiently explained by cell-intrinsic activation patterns and bacterial burden $(7,8)$. In wild-type (wt) mice, S. aureus intradermal (id) infection was selfresolving within 1 week (Fig. 1A). Concomitant with this, skin neutrophils and IL-1 $\beta$ tissue concentrations peaked at 1 day post-infection (dpi) and then waned until 7 dpi (Fig. 1B and fig. S1G). To comprehensively map dynamic changes across canonical immune cell types, we performed high parametric flow cytometry combined with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) (28) dimensionality reduction and FlowSOM meta-clustering (29) on extracted tissue cells from mice infected with S. aureus in both ears for 1, S, and 7 days. This approach revealed highly complex kinetic profiles of 17 immune cell populations in control and infected mice (fig. S1, A and B). At 7 dpi, CD4, CD8, and $\mathrm{CD} 4^{-} \mathrm{CD} 8^{-} \alpha \beta$ T cells in the dermis steadily increased in number, similarly to V $\gamma 6$ $\gamma \delta$ T cells, whereas V $\gamma 4 \gamma \delta$ T cells increased until 5 dpi before decreasing at 7 dpi (fig. S1C). In contrast, B cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), and mast cells remained relatively constant in number (fig. S1D). By 5 to 7 dpi natural killer (NK) cells and eosinophils accumulated in the tissue (fig. S1E), as did dendritic cells (DCs), monocytes, and CD64 ${ }^{\text {Hi }}$ Macs (fig. S1F). Dermal CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs, signaling via MyD88, are essential for bacterial clearance (7). To gain insight into the signaling pathways that mediate infection clearance beyond MyD88 $(7,8)$, we sorted CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ dermal Macs and performed RNA sequencing (RNAseq). Despite the self-limiting course of the infection (7), we found large changes in gene expression in the dermal Macs compartment with 4034, 4726, and 5993 differentially expressed genes on days 1,5 , and 7 , respectively, as compared with Macs from control mice (fig. S1H). Next, we expanded our immunophenotyping beyond CD64 (used to identify dermal Macs in fig. S1A) by including CD206, ty-rosine-protein kinase MER (MERTK), and major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II). This approach revealed the heterogeneity of dermal Macs because we identified five distinct clusters over the course of infection (Fig. 1, C to F). During homeostasis, CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs could be divided into CD206 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ and CD206 ${ }^{\text {Int }}$ subsets (Fig. 1C and fig. S1I) (12). In addition, cells coexpressing CD64 and Ly6C were present in the steady-state dermis (Fig. 1, C and D), suggesting a developmental pathway from infiltrating monocytes. This agreed with our previous data demonstrating that a large fraction of resident Macs are continuously renewed by tissue-homing Ly6C ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ monocytes, which up-regulate CD64, whereas a population of embryonically derived, nerve-associated Macs remains until adulthood $(7,8)$. At 1 dpi , monocyte-derived Macs infiltrated the dermis, as indicated by a notable increase in cells coexpressing CD64 and Ly6C (Fig. 1, C and D, and fig. S1I). At later time points, an increase in the Macs expressing MHC-II potentially reflected enhanced interactions with adaptive immune cells. We also observed the up-regulation of arginase 1 (ARG1)and nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2)-expressing Macs at 5 or 7 dpi, indicative of activation (Fig. 1, C and D, and fig. S1I). We next determined whether prior resident and newly recruited Macs differed in their inflammatory response to staphylococci and whether differences in marker expression at the Mac population level (such as MHC-II, NOS2, or ARG1) resulted from preferential expression by specific subsets with distinct origins. Thus, we examined Cxcr4 ${ }^{\text {CreERT2/+: }} R 26^{\text {CAG-LSL-tdT }}$ mice, where HSC-derived monocytes (but not CD206 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs) are labeled by induction with tamoxifen (TAM) (fig. S1J, top) (30). We induced with TAM 1 week before infection and could distinguish Macs already present in the tissue (Tomato ${ }^{\mathrm{Lo}}$ ) and those newly recruited (Tomato ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ ). At steady state, $\sim 15 \%$ of CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs were Tomato ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$, which increased to $\sim 50 \%$ at 1 dpi (Fig. 1, G and H). We observed increased Il1b expression in both Mac subsets (Fig. 1I), albeit with higher expression in the newly recruited cells. Accordingly, we observed pro-IL-1 $\beta$ expression, analyzed by intracellular staining at 1 dpi , in both CD206 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ and Ly6C ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ subsets, although the response was more robust within Ly6C ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs (Fig. 1, J and K). In addition, in Cxcr4 ${ }^{\text {CreERT2/+: }} R 26^{\text {CAG-LSL-tdT }}$ mice, both NOS2 and ARG1 were increased in Tomato ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs on 5 and 7 dpi (Fig. 1L and fig. S1K). To complement these data, we analyzed Mrc1 ${ }^{\text {CreERT2/CreERT2 }}$ :R26 ${ }^{\text {CAG-LSL-tdT }}$ mice (31). In these mice, TAM induction labels CD206-expressing cells. About $85 \%$ of the CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs expressed Tomato 1 week after TAM induction in steady state (Fig. 1M), whereas Ly6C ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs remained unlabeled (fig. S1J, lower). After infection, the frequency of Tomato ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ cells decreased (Fig. 1N). Tomato ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs (i.e., those present before infection) also up-regulated NOS2 and ARG1 at 5 and 7 dpi (Fig. 1O and fig. S1L). Similarly, at 5 dpi, both Tomato-positive (prior resident) and -negative (newly recruited) Macs showed increased MHC-II expression (Fig. 1, P and Q). These data indicated that a self-limiting $S$. aureus infection induces dynamic changes in the immune cell composition of the skin and that both prior resident and newly recruited Macs robustly respond during infection. ## Dermal Mac reprogramming is initiated by GM-CSF Because we previously found that very early immune events in skin infection determine later outcomes (8), we focused on signaling pathways up-regulated in CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ dermal Macs at 1 dpi. To examine whether these groups also differed in terms of their HIF-1 $\alpha$ requirement to induce glycolysis, we generated BMDMs from wt and Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$mice using either M-CSF or GM-CSF. MCSF Hif1 $\alpha^{-/-}$BMDMs had reduced expression of Slc2a1 compared with wt cells, used less glucose, and secreted less lactate after both stimulation with hf or infection with live S. aureus (Fig. 5D). Moreover, Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$BMDMs were impaired in mounting an effective inflammatory response as determined by nitric oxide (NO) and IL-1 $\beta$ production (Fig. 5E). In contrast, BMDMs generated in GMCSF displayed a HIF-1 $\alpha$-independent phenotype. No difference in Slc2a1 expression was observed, whereas glucose uptake and lactate secretion were comparable to wt cells (Fig. 5F), as were NO and IL$1 \beta$ production (Fig. 5G). In addition, extracellular flux analysis revealed that M-CSF Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$BMDMs had reduced glycolysis, whereas HIF-1 $\alpha$ deficiency did not affect glycolysis in GM-CSF BMDMs (fig. S5F). Last, wt M-CSF Macs treated with the HIF-1 $\alpha$ inhibitor CAY10585 produced less NO in response to live S. aureus, whereas GM-CSF Macs were unaffected (fig. S5G). Moreover, pulsing of Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$M-CSF-derived BMDMs with GM-CSF for 24 hours (setup depicted in fig. S5C) was sufficient to overrule HIF-1 $\alpha$ deficiency and resulted in comparable levels of lactate secretion upon S. aureus stimulation in wt and HIF1a ${ }^{-/-}$BMDMs (fig. S5H). To complement the above data, we incubated human induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSC)-derived Macs in either human (hu) M-CSF or huGM-CSF. After an incubation period of 3 days, the cells were harvested and stimulated with live S. aureus in the presence or absence of a HIF-1 $\alpha$ inhibitor, and their glycolytic capacity was measured. Infected IPSC-derived Macs up-regulated glycolysis as compared with controls regardless of whether they were cultured in huM-CSF or huGM-CSF. However, only the cells cultured in huM-CSF were susceptible to HIF-1 $\alpha$ inhibition, as indicated by reduced extracellular acidification rate. In contrast, and in agreement with our BMDM data, IPSC-derived Macs cultured in huGM-CSF did not require HIF-1 $\alpha$ for optimal glycolysis (fig. S5I). Because HIF-1 $\alpha$ is a key player in the cellular response to hypoxia $(46,47)$, we wondered whether GM-CSF-derived Macs would maintain their HIF-1 $\alpha$-independent phenotype even under lowoxygen conditions. We analyzed wt BMDMs on an extracellular flux analyzer placed inside a hypoxia chamber ( $1 \%$ oxygen). GMCSF BMDMs incubated for 2 hours at $1 \%$ oxygen had increased glycolysis compared with M-CSF-derived Macs, suggesting an enhanced ability to respond to hypoxic conditions (fig. S5J). Moreover, whereas $1 \%$ oxygen up-regulated the expression of Slc2a1 and Slc16a3 irrespective of whether wt BMDMs were cultured in M-CSF or GM-CSF, only GM-CSF Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$, but not MCSF Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$, BMDMs up-regulated both genes in low oxygen (Fig. 5, H to J). Lastly, M-CSF Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$BMDMs incubated in low oxygen took up less glucose and secreted less lactate than wt cells upon stimulation (Fig. 5K and fig. S5K), whereas Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$and wt BMDMs cultured in GM-CSF did not differ (Fig. 5L and fig. S5K). As was the case in normoxic conditions, short-term pulsing of MCSF Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$BMDMs with GM-CSF rescued the impairment of glycolysis in these cells (Fig. 5M). Thus, GM-CSF Macs did not require HIF-1 $\alpha$ for glycolysis up-regulation even under lowoxygen conditions. However, it remained puzzling that GM-CSF Macs did not require HIF-1 $\alpha$ and that dermal Macs were reprogrammed by GM-CSF during infection, yet bacterial clearance was impaired in Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$mice at 5 dpi . We hypothesized that HIF-1 $\alpha$ was required at the very early stages of infection before GM-CSF imprinted dermal Macs. Accordingly, we infected mice for 6 hours with S. aureus. Whereas Mac numbers did not differ in wt and Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$mice in steady state (fig. S5L), Mac numbers were reduced in Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$mice 6 hours after infection (fig. S5M). Therefore, we analyzed the kinetics of TCA cycle metabolites of S. aureus-stimulated BMDMs. We found lactate, pyruvate, succinate, fumarate, itaconate, and malate all to be increased by 24 hours when the Mac autonomous response was at its peak (fig. S6, A and D). In the case of itaconate, this seemed intriguing because it has previously been suggested as a negative regulator of TLR-mediated cytokine activation (49). Accordingly, we further explored itaconate and its regulation and found that $S$. aureus induced the expression of Irg1 and the synthesis of itaconate in both M-CSF and GM-CSF BMDMs in a HIF-1 $\alpha$-independent manner (Fig. 6, A and B and fig. S6, B and C). Irg1 expression and itaconate synthesis were induced by GM-CSF BMDMs already at baseline (Fig. 6, A and B, and fig. S6E). Because itaconate is derived from cis-aconitate in the TCA cycle, its baseline production likely explains the increased glutamine uptake in GM-CSF BMDMs (fig. S5E). Stable isotope labeling using ${ }^{13} \mathrm{C}$ glucose revealed that itaconate was, in part, derived from glucose in steady state as well as in stimulated GM-CSF and M-CSF BMDMs (fig. S6F). We next wondered what was driving Irg1 expression in steady-state GM-CSF BMDMs. IFN- $\beta$ has previously been reported to induce itaconate in LPS-activated BMDMs (50). However, the steady-state expression of Ifnb was similar in MCSF and GM-CSF BMDMs (fig. S6G). Also, no difference in steady-state Irg1 expression was observed between wt and Ifnar ${ }^{-/-}$GM-CSF BMDMs (fig. S6H), indicating mediators beyond IFN- $\beta$. Instead, GM-CSF BMDMs had increased expression of Tnf (fig. S6I) and secreted TNF protein in steady state (fig. S6J). GM-CSF BMDMs from Tnfr1 ${ }^{-/-}$mice had impaired expression of Irg1 compared with wt cells (fig. S6K), suggesting that autocrine TNF signaling may drive itaconate synthesis. To assess the function of itaconate in regulating Mac activity during infection, we analyzed the cytokine response to S. aureus (and LPS) in $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$M-CSF or GM-CSF BMDMs. IRG1 deficiency in M-CSF BMDMs resulted in similar IL-6 but increased TNF and IL-1 $\beta$ levels (fig. S6L). However, both TNF and IL-1 $\beta$ were reduced in $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$GM-CSF BMDMs in response to S. aureus as compared with wt BMDM (fig. S6M). Accordingly, in contrast to the situation in M-CSF Macs, itaconate is required for an optimal response to $S$. aureus by GM-CSF Macs. Next, we explored whether itaconate was relevant during $S$. aureus skin infection. Dermal Macs up-regulated the expression of Irg1 after infection (Fig. 6C), whereas itaconate was detected in Macs sorted from wt mice at 7 dpi (Fig. 6D). To determine the relevance of this, we infected wt and $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice with S. aureus. In contrast to Hif1a ${ }^{-/-}$mice, $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice did not have reduced CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs at 6 hours post-infection (Fig. 6E). Similarly, at 1 dpi, both groups had comparable bacterial loads (Fig. 6F) and Mac frequencies (fig. S6N). However, at 5 dpi, PML and bacteria were increased in $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$as compared with wt mice (Fig. 6, H and I) without differences in Mac frequencies (Fig. 6G and fig. S6O). To investigate preferential itaconate utilization by Mac subsets, we analyzed BM chimeras with wt or $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$BM transferred to $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$or wt mice. S. aureus infection 8 weeks after transfer revealed, at 5 dpi , an increased bacterial burden in the wt-to$\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$group as compared with $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$-to-wt and wt-to-wt conditions (Fig. 6J). To exclude that direct antimicrobial properties of itaconate affected in vivo infection (51), the growth of S. aureus cultured in LB media with or without itaconic acid was analyzed and found not to differ (Fig. 6K). Next, we applied 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI) directly to the ears of $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice before infection (Fig. 6L). Early after infection (1 dpi), bacterial numbers were similar in wt and $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice that had received either 4-OI or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Fig. 6M). At 5 dpi, 4-OI-treated $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice had reduced Macs (Fig. 6N) and bacterial burden as compared with infected $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice without 4-OI, whereas skin PML were almost completely absent (Fig. 6O). In addition, the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 was increased in tissue lysates from these mice (Fig. 6P). To establish the source of IL-10, we treated mice as depicted in Fig. 6L, generated single-cell suspensions, and performed intracellular IL-10 staining. We identified CD4 and regulatory T cells, as well as DCs and CD64 ${ }^{\mathrm{Hi}}$ Macs, as sources of IL-10 (Fig. 6, Q and R) (markers used to identify the analyzed populations are depicted in fig. S6, P and Q). Last, to gain insight into the profound effect of 4-OI on infection resolution, dermal Macs were sorted at 1 dpi. Macs from DMSOtreated $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice had increased expression of several inflammatory genes as compared with Macs sorted from infected wt mice. The expression levels of these genes were restored to wt levels in dermal Macs sorted from 4-OI-treated $\operatorname{Irg1}^{-/-}$mice, whereas 4 OI also blunted the expression of Il1b (Fig. 6S). Collectively, these results indicate that itaconate is broadly required to modulate inflammatory gene expression by Macs during infection. ## DISCUSSION In mucocutaneous barriers, direct contact between dermal Macs and S. aureus occurs on a daily basis. Tightly regulated response patterns in Macs are required to encounter these frequent challenges while preserving long-term tissue homeostasis. In the steady state, dermal Macs require M-CSF for at-site differentiation and maintenance (9). However, in bacterial infection, GM-CSF, which is initially derived from skin resident $\gamma \delta \mathrm{T}$ cells, diverts dermal Macs away from a homeostatic M-CSF program for the acquisition of distinct immunometabolic properties. With the help of fate mapping, we found that, although GM-CSF acted on both resident and newly recruited Macs, the latter responded much more robustly. Our BM transfer experiments supported this because the transfer of Csf2rb-deficient BM decreased bacterial resistance in wt mice. This association of recent history of provenance and initial conditioning in a homeostatic versus an inflammatory environment correlated with differences in localization. DMacs, dermal Macs. DM, DMSO.Thus, the vicinity to $\gamma \delta \mathrm{T}$ cells may be a critical factor in Macs tuning. GM-CSF was nonredundant in this context because dermal Macs sorted from GM-CSF receptor-deficient mice failed to mount a sufficient inflammatory response, because they were incapable of clearing the infection in a timely fashion. Furthermore, we identify GM-CSF as a key regulator of innate immune memory in the skin, although other factors are likely to essentially contribute. Whereas a central role of intrinsic metabolic changes in immune cell activation has been firmly established in recent years, the bulk of the data have been generated in vitro (38). Whereas these approaches provide valuable molecular information (particularly because, due to low cell numbers, dermal Macs cannot be used in many metabolic assays, e.g., Seahorse analysis), they fall short of depicting the complexity of intercellular networks, especially during infection where the immune cell composition and single-cell states alter dynamically. As a notable example, the transcription factor HIF-1 $\alpha$ has a central role in homeostatic dermal Macs for initiating the immune response in staphylococcal infection, in line with its established central position in allowing for the glycolytic switch in inflammatory Macs in vitro. Yet, by 1 dpi , GM-CSF signaling allowed Macs to bypass the requirement for HIF-1 $\alpha$, even under hypoxic conditions. The central role of GM-CSF in fine-tuning Mac metabolism is underlined by our unexpected observation, that it alone induces Irg1 expression and itaconate generation in vitro, in a partly TNF-dependent fashion. It seems an intriguing hypothesis that GM-CSF discretely conditions subsets of Macs in one tissue for optimal adaptation to metabolic restrictions and to the chance of infectious encounters. Our data on GM-CSF-producing T cells approaching Macs in staphylococcal skin infection make this a highly plausible scenario. Whether and how the outlined axis of GM-CSF and itaconate affects resident Macs which require GMCSF in vivo, in particular alveolar Macs, remains to be explored. Next to GM-CSF, we identified the formation of itaconate to be a potent tuning mechanism in staphylococcal infection. The immunomodulatory properties of itaconate have been previously appreciated, mostly using in vitro models $(49,50,52)$, with increasing evidence in vivo (53-56). BM chimeras revealed increased bacterial loads in the wt-to-Irg1 $1^{-/-}$group as compared with controls, whereas no significant difference was observed when $\operatorname{Irg} 1^{-/-}$BM was transferred to wt animals. The combination of approaches, including bone marrow chimeras, applied in this study suggests that itaconate synthesis by prior resident Macs as compared with incoming Macs may be particularly relevant during infection resolution. The mechanistic reason for a differential requirement of GM-CSF signaling and itaconate synthesis by prior resident and newly recruited Macs is currently unclear and will require further study. The fact that a slight delay in Macs activation results in substantially increased inflammation 5 days later strongly supports a model where IRG1 is critical for an early robust cytokine response by GMCSF-primed Macs involving itaconate as an activity-promoting metabolite. In line with this, impairment of staphylococcal infection resolution in $\operatorname{Irg} 1^{-/-}$mice could be compensated for by the local application of 4-OI directly to the skin before infection with complex Mac reprogramming. The potential of 4-OI in directing inflammation at the site of infection offers translational perspectives for exploiting immunometabolic Macs properties in tissue infection, thus expanding the therapeutic potential of metabolites $(57,58)$. We show that Macs adopt a GM-CSF-dependent transcriptional program during infection. However, it should be noted that we cannot conclude that M-CSF receptor down-regulation equates to nonfunctionality in dermal macs. In addition, we show that GM-CSF-conditioned Macs exhibit a HIF-1 $\alpha$-independent phenotype, yet the precise mechanism for this is currently unknown and requires further investigation. We observe that local 4-OI treatment modulates gene expression in Macs. However, it is likely to also affect other immune as well as stromal cells in the skin. Further investigation is needed to understand the impact of 4-OI on cells beyond dermal Macs. This is especially vital if exploring the therapeutic potential of 4-OI in skin diseases. Last, our work indicates a potentially essential role for type 1 IFNs which peak late in infection, when bacteria have already largely been cleared from the tissue. Currently, underlying regulatory mechanisms and the functional consequences of the late type 1 IFNs are unclear and should be the subject of future studies. In summary, we demonstrate that, during staphylococcal skin infection, dermal Macs are subjected to local hypoxia and TLR activation. This engages several sequential and interwoven signaling pathways, both in resident and in newly recruited Macs, all of which are critical for infection resolution. This Mac program represents a bottleneck in antimicrobial resistance, inflammation control, and temporal tissue immune memory and may contain molecular targets for therapeutic interventions. ## MATERIALS AND METHODS ## Study design This study investigated dermal Mac intrinsic signaling pathways and microenvironmental changes in S. aureus skin infection. After restimulation, surface labeling was performed by incubating the cells with antibodies in PBS at $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for 20 min . Next, cells were fixed and permeabilized with $100 \mu \mathrm{l}$ of BD Cytofix/Cytoperm solution at $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for 20 min . Afterward, cells were washed and labeled intracellularly at $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in a permeabilization buffer overnight. Data acquisition was performed on a 5L Cytek Aurora (Cytek), and Fcs files were analyzed using FlowJo software (Tree Star). Antibodies are listed in Supplementary Materials and Methods. ## High-dimensional analysis High-dimensional analysis was performed as described previously (60). In short, raw files were preprocessed using FlowJo. Compensated CD45 ${ }^{+}$, live single cells were exported from FlowJo and imported into R studio. Transformation and percentile normalization were performed to obtain values between 0 and 1. This was followed by dimensionality reduction and visualization by UMAP. A FlowSOM algorithm was used for automated clustering and meta-clustering, followed by expert-guided merging of some clusters using the information from the heatmap with median expression values and the UMAP with overlayed expression values. ## Immunofluorescence analysis of whole-tissue mounts For immunofluorescence analysis of whole ear mounts, mice were euthanized, and ears were cut at the hairline. The ears were split into dorsal and ventral parts and incubated in 24 -well plates overnight in1 ml of $1 \%$ paraformaldehyde at $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in the dark, then incubated overnight in wash buffer ( $1 \%$ bovine serum albumin, $0.1 \%$ Triton $\mathrm{X}-100,4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ). After mechanical removal of cartilage, the ears were stained in $200 \mu \mathrm{l}$ of wash buffer overnight at $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then washed three times ( 5 min on a rocking table). The ears were then mounted on microscopy slides in ProLong Diamond, allowed to dry overnight, and analyzed on a Zeiss LSM 880 AiryScan confocal microscope using a $20 \times, 40 \times$, or $63 \times$ objective. ImageJ was used to quantify the signal intensity of whole mounts stained with anti-pimonidazole antibodies. For 3D reconstruction, Imaris cell imaging software was used. ## RNA-seq BMDMs in M-CSF cultures were defined as being for CD11b and F4/80. In GM-CSF cultures, the BMDMs were defined as CD115 ${ }^{\text {Hi }}$ and MHC-II ${ }^{\mathrm{Lo}}$. After sorting, BMDMs were seeded at $1 \times 10^{6}$ cells per well into six-well plates in medium with M-CSF or GM-CSF (20 $\mathrm{ng} / \mathrm{ml}$ ). The next day, the BMDMs were stimulated with $1 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{ml}$ of hf $S$. aureus for 4 hours. The cells were washed, harvested with gentle scraping, pelleted, and lysed in $350 \mu \mathrm{l}$ of RLT buffer (Qiagen) with $1 \% \beta$-mercaptoethanol. RNA was extracted with RNeasy MicroKit according to the manufacturer's instructions (Qiagen). Sample processing was performed by CeGaT (Center for Genomics and Transcriptomics, Tübingen, Germany). Library preparation was performed with 100 ng of quality-controlled RNA using the TruSeq Stranded mRNA kit (Illumina). A Q30 value of $94.4 \%$ was reached. Demultiplexing of the sequencing reads was performed with Illumina bcl2fastq (2.19). Adapters were trimmed with Skewer (version 0.2.2) (61). Trimmed raw reads were aligned to reference genome mm10 using STAR (version 2.5.2b) (62). Differential expression analysis between groups was performed with DESeq2 (63) in R (R Core Team 2015). For dermal Macs, wt mice were infected for 1, 5, and 7 days or left uninfected. Dermal Macs were sorted from the ear and lysed in 350 $\mu \mathrm{l}$ of RLT buffer supplemented with $1 \% \beta$-mercaptoethanol. The RNA was extracted using the RNeasy MicroKit according to the manufacturer's instructions (Qiagen). Paired-end sequencing of the quality-controlled library was carried out with NovaSeq 6000. Demultiplexing of sequenced reads was performed with Illumina bcl2fastq (version 2.19) and adapter trimming with Cutadapt (64). The raw reads were subsequently mapped to the mm10 murine reference genome with STAR (Version 2.5.2b) (62) and counted with feature counts (65). The obtained counted reads were processed using the DESeq2 package (63). Heatmaps were generated with Morpheus (https://software. broadinstitute.org/morpheus/). GO enrichment analysis was performed using the PANTHER classification database (66) on regulated ( $P_{\text {adj }}<0.05$ and $>2 \log _{2}$ fold change expression) genes. Volcano plots were generated in R on genes with a $P<0.05$ and $>2 \log _{2}$ fold change expression. Datasets have been uploaded to the GEO platform (accession number: GSE174676). ## Quantification and statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed with GraphPad Prism (GraphPad software, Version 8 or 9). For the comparison of the two groups, an unpaired two-tailed Student's $t$ test or Mann-Whitney test was applied. For multiple comparisons, one- or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed, followed by Tukey's multiple comparison or Dunnett's multiple comparison tests. Differences were considered statistically significant when ${ }^{*} P \leq 0.05,{ }^{* *} P \leq 0.01$, ${ }^{* * *} P \leq 0.001$, and ${ }^{* * * *} P \leq 0.0001$. Data are presented as means $\pm$ SEM if not stated otherwise. ## Supplementary Materials This PDF file includes: Materials and Methods Figs.
